lines: Thunder rattled every blade on the wall before I could secure the rack.
I covered the grindstone and moved the finished weapons away from the windows.
Lightning struck close enough to leave my hammer humming in my hand.
The bell sounded thin under that sky, but it still brought everyone indoors.
Rain came through the forge roof and landed beside the quench bucket.
I checked the workshop first, then went door to door with the others.
One shutter tore loose and scattered half my charcoal across the floor.
The apprentices flinched at every flash. I kept them busy checking handles.
A fallen branch blocked the armory door until we cut it apart.
No blade is useful against weather like that. Dry shelter was the better defense.
The golem stood in the square through the whole storm. Its judgment remains questionable.
I wrapped the weapon grips in cloth before the damp could reach them.
A lightning strike split the fence near the watch post. We replaced the rails this morning.
The storm ended, but the steel kept ticking as the room cooled.
I found water under the weapon chest and rust on nothing. We were lucky.
Several guards brought their gear in soaked and expected miracles by sunrise.
Today every blade gets dried, oiled, and checked for a loose fitting.
Thunder makes even a sound weapon feel small in the hand.
I spent more time calming neighbors than protecting the forge. That was the right choice.
Next storm, the roof gets checked before the clouds reach us.
Smoke reached the forge before the flames did.
I shut the bellows, covered the coals, and joined the bucket line.
A weaponsmith knows controlled fire. That village blaze had no control in it.
We moved the oil and charcoal before the wind could carry sparks our way.
The heat warped two weapon racks even though the flames never touched them.
I used the longest tongs I own to pull burning boards from the doorway.
People came first. The unfinished blades stayed where they were.
A guard used a shield to cover someone from falling embers. It will need a new face.
We soaked the forge roof while the bucket line fought the next house.
The hammer handles smell of smoke, but none of the tools were lost.
I saw neighbors run toward the well before anyone told them what to do.
One hot blade was left on the bench when the alarm rang. I found it cold beside the ash.
The fire jumped the lane on a shower of sparks. Wet blankets stopped it at the fence.
I checked every coal after the flames were out. Then I checked them again.
Several weapons came back scorched from the rescue work, and every one can be repaired.
The forge feels different after seeing fire where it does not belong.
We lost a shed full of supplies, but everyone inside made it out.
Today I am replacing dried grips and cleaning soot from the fittings.
A bucket carried with both hands mattered more than any sword that night.
I will keep the coal bins farther from the wall from now on.
The first horn sounded while a sword was still turning on the grindstone.
I opened the weapon chest and handed out only what each defender could control.
Blades came back chipped after every wave, and I repaired the worst ones first.
The bell got the families indoors while we formed a line at the gate.
A sharp edge helped, but steady footing held the narrow lane.
I watched a frightened guard lower their weapon until a neighbor cleared the way.
The golem took three bolts meant for people behind it.
We ran out of spare shields before we ran out of defenders.
I carried a hammer to the gate and spent more time fixing the bar than swinging it.
Raiders tested the east entrance twice. It will be reinforced before sunset.
One axe split at the handle because its owner ignored an old crack.
The wounded left their weapons by the door, and someone always took their place.
I heard the last horn and still waited before putting the tools down.
The forge stayed hot through the night because repair work could not wait.
Every nick I cleaned this morning belongs to someone who reached home.
Nobody needs a heroic blade. They need sound weapons and people who stand together.
We recovered most of the gear from the square after the fighting stopped.
The gate held because the defenders kept their line instead of chasing raiders.
Before another raid, I want every grip, bowstring, and shield strap inspected.
The village survived the raid. The weapon racks show exactly what it cost.
The first cry came from beyond the last torch, and every weapon rack emptied at once.
I lit the forge so defenders could find the workshop through the dark.
A loose grip is dangerous in daylight and worse when you cannot see your hand.
I handed out short weapons because the lanes were too tight for wide swings.
The golem kept turning toward footsteps none of us could place.
We set spare blades by the watch posts and lanterns beside every door.
One guard reached me with a broken shield and no idea where the blow came from.
The dark made every fence shadow look like another attacker.
I stayed near the square and checked each weapon before it changed hands.
A torch went out on the east path, so we held that corner with sound and patience.
Nobody chased movement beyond the lights. That restraint kept people alive.
The doors shook until dawn, and so did the tools hanging on the wall.
We found claw marks on the workshop door after sunrise.
I cleaned mud from the blades and blood from one hammer handle.
Several defenders gripped too tightly and could barely open their hands afterward.
The first quiet minute felt wrong because we had listened for danger all night.
Today I am repairing lantern hooks before I touch the damaged steel.
A weapon only helps if the watch spots trouble soon enough to use it.
Tonight every dark gap between the houses gets another torch.
The attack ended at dawn, but nobody at the forge slept after it.
Sand reached the grindstone before I could cover it.
I wrapped every blade and moved the weapon racks away from the doors.
Grit worked into the hinges, the sheaths, and every drop of oil I had open.
We tied cloth over our faces and followed the wall across the square.
A weaponsmith can hear one grain of sand scraping where it should not be.
The sky turned brown enough that the forge fire looked pale.
I shut the bellows before they filled the coals with dust.
Two guards brought their weapons in bare. Both edges will need patient cleaning.
Sand packed around the armory door until three of us forced it open.
The wind knocked a spear rack flat, but nobody was standing beneath it.
I used the oil cloths to cover faces before I covered the steel.
Every moving fitting sounded rough by the time the storm passed.
The village disappeared beyond the workshop window for most of the afternoon.
We marked the forge door with a lantern so lost neighbors could find shelter.
No weapon was drawn during the storm. Keeping them clean was trouble enough.
The air cleared, and the whole workshop kept making a grinding sound.
Today every sheath gets emptied and every hinge gets brushed clean.
The watch posts need covers if we expect gear to survive another storm.
Sand can ruin a weapon quietly, one scratch at a time.
I will keep sealed oil and spare cloth ready before the next hard wind.
Snow blocked the forge door before the morning fire was hot.
I warmed the grips slowly so the leather would not crack.
Cold made the steel painful to hold even through gloves.
We moved the weapon racks away from the wall where frost had formed.
I left the grindstone still and helped clear the path to the meeting house.
A frozen hand has no business carrying a blade.
The guards brought their gear inside under blankets to keep ice off the fittings.
Snow covered the watch path, so we marked it with spare spear shafts.
The bell rope froze stiff until three of us worked it loose.
One roof beam began to bend under the weight, and everyone left before it broke.
I used the forge to warm neighbors, not steel, for most of the night.
The woodpile fell low enough that unfinished work became firewood.
Ice formed inside two sheaths and held the blades fast.
We tied a rope between the forge and the nearest homes before visibility vanished.
The golem collected snow until it looked like a moving hill.
Morning found every axe busy on ice and fallen branches.
I checked the quiet houses before reopening the workshop.
Today every weapon gets dried before rust finds the hidden seams.
The village stayed warm because people shared fuel instead of guarding their own stacks.
Before the next storm, I want dry gloves stored beside every weapon rack.
After a raid, every blade in the village feels too dull and too late.
I am still sorting what happened. The forge sounds different after a raid.
We count people first. Bent weapons can wait.
I heard the first horn while a blade was still on the stone.
Every guard came back with a different account and a new nick in the steel.
The bell got everyone inside before the raiders reached the square.
Bolts struck the walls hard enough to shake dust from the rafters.
I saw neighbors hold a narrow lane with farm tools and nerve.
Some weapons came back broken. Some never came back at all.
I repaired hilts until sunrise and still felt behind.
Raiders tested every entrance, so next time we reinforce every one.
The golem bought us time that no blade could have bought alone.
I can clean blood from steel. I cannot forget who carried it home.
The quiet after the last wave was worse than the horns.
Before the next raid, every village weapon gets checked twice.
Discipline kept the defenders together when anger would have scattered them.
A sharp weapon matters, but knowing where to stand matters more.
I remember the sound of the gate holding under one more charge.
We survived because people covered one another instead of chasing glory.
The raid ended. The repair work did not.
